text:
Chapter Thirty-Two


For the first time in weeks, Maggie left her apartment early so she could spend Monday morning alone in her office. After dinner on Saturday, she had returned to Galloway by herself, leaving Arthur in Atlantia with his family. Alone, she could not stop thinking about what Lane had said. It ran through her mind on repeat, and with each repetition, she grew more and more anxious about what it meant. Either Arthur had told Lane about her, or her affection for him was so obvious that Lane suspected. Either possibility had Maggie on edge.


She never should have agreed to the baseball game, to dinner with his family. It was too intimate, the kind of thing you did with someone you were going to stay with, not for a relationship that had an expiration date. And her relationship with Arthur had to have an expiration date—didn’t it?


What if it didn’t? How could she fit Arthur into her life? Easily, her mind supplied, only too eager to spin out the fairy tale. Long days on campus that ended in dinner at Dot’s; the walk back to her apartment hand in hand; coffee at Bean There, Done That on Sunday mornings as they graded papers, followed by an afternoon sitting on the second floor of Willoughby’s. Simon’s baseball games in the summer, trips to the beach, and endless hours spent reading side by side. It ached to dream about, when she knew she wasn’t brave enough to risk it.


And, at some point, her fears stopped being just about what she would lose in an inevitable breakup. Arthur had just as much to lose as she did. Maybe they would date for six months or a year or two, until their happiness curdled. And then what would happen when they broke up after their lives were already braided together?


It was just as easy for her mind to spin this nightmare. Arthur was too kind, too good. If they broke up and couldn’t work side by side, he would leave Hawthorn. And what would he do then? He needed to be close to this precious family he had, the thing he had wanted for so long. She couldn’t take that away from him. Couldn’t take him away from Simon and Rory or Barry and Lane.


She looked over at his empty desk, at the photo of Arthur, Rory, and Simon. He had texted her that he was on his way, driving the winding roads from Atlantia. He had messaged that he couldn’t wait to see her and that he’d pick up a coffee at Bean There. All she wanted was to wrap him in her arms when he arrived, but she knew she couldn’t. She knew he would feel the tension radiating from her. She was never very good at hiding what was on her mind.


She dropped her head into her hands. She was exhausted. Her eyes were red-rimmed and aching, and her chest hurt. She had slept fitfully on Saturday and Sunday night, too caught up in her anxious spiral to rest, the screeches from banshees from deep in the Wilds reminding her of everything else that was at stake. What had she done?


A tapping knock on her office door startled her out of her misery. Dean Clearwater stood in the hall holding a file folder. He wore his summer attire—jeans and a Hawthorn Splinters shirt under a blazer—but his mouth was set in a hard line.


“Good morning. Is Dr. Taliesin here?” He was strangely stiff as he looked around her office, as if Arthur might be hiding in the space behind the open door or beneath her desk.


“No.” Her voice was scratchy, worn out from crying and little sleep. “He’s on his way, though. He should be here in half an hour. Should I tell him to come to Ferox Hall first?”


The deep wrinkle in his forehead grew deeper. “No, that’s fine. I’m sure he has a busy schedule today. This concerns you as much as him, anyway.” He placed the file folder on her desk, tapping it once and sliding it over to her. “Please let him know that the paperwork has been filed and approved by the board. His grant is fully funded.”


Maggie had never heard Arthur talk about a grant, and she had no idea what it would have to do with her. She opened the file folder, trying to understand. “What am I looking at?”


“Apparently, there was some kind of budgeting error. Were you aware?”


Maggie swallowed, her throat dry. Arthur had promised he wouldn’t talk to Dean Clearwater. Why would he break that promise? “I was,” she admitted.


“And did you complain to Dr. Taliesin about the error? I understand your project was defunded, and that’s very disappointing.” Maggie couldn’t hide the way her lip curled in anger; she was too tired. He was talking to her like she was a child. Like she was irrational for being upset. “But I think my expectations about how you were to approach your relationship with Dr. Taliesin were clear.”


“I took what you said very seriously,” she argued. “I am helping him at the expense of my own work. We have a very good working relationship.”


“Then why is Dr. Taliesin concerned about a budgeting error instead of the pall that is still growing in this building?” The implication in his words was clear. You asked him to do this. You put him up to it.


“I didn’t…I had nothing to do with this.” She held up the file folder as she said it before setting it down to look at its contents again. Oh, Arthur…The grant was an annual gift of twelve thousand dollars, earmarked for her seminar, even more than was originally awarded to the program. “Where did this money come from?”


Dean Clearwater narrowed his eyes. “Dr. Taliesin funded this himself. Why would he do that, Maggie?” Anger burned, hot and shameful, in her gut. Arthur hadn’t stopped to think, not for one moment, what this would look like to the dean. He hadn’t listened to her. He’d gone behind her back and broken his promise to wait. She was a fool.


“If you’re implying that I asked him to use his own money to fund a grant—”


“What did you ask him?” Dean Clearwater interrupted.


Maggie rubbed her eyes. She was so tired. “I asked him to reconsider the budget at the committee meeting in the fall. That’s it.” She looked over at Dean Clearwater. “I know how hard it is to get funding back on a project once it’s been taken away. I didn’t want special treatment. I just wanted my seminar back.”


“Maggie.” The dean’s voice was almost gentle, even with its hard edge. “Is there anything I need to know?”


“No,” she said, too quickly. The dean’s impressive eyebrows arched, but it was clear to her now what she needed to do. “We are going to get rid of the pall as soon as the gloaming creeper decoction is ready, and everything will go back to the way it was.” She paused. “What about the grant?”


He looked down at her over his bifocals. “I told you it was approved by the board of trustees. Please let Dr. Taliesin know.”


After a moment when he watched her with an exacting gaze, he turned to leave. As he reached the door, Maggie called out to him. “Why did you put him in this office?”


Dean Clearwater’s eyes softened, only slightly. “You weren’t my first choice,” he said. “But I didn’t make the office assignments. Dr. Taliesin did. I tried to get him to reconsider, but he insisted.”


The knot of nerves in her stomach tightened and her cheeks burned hotter. Dahlia had been right, all along. What had Arthur been thinking? Gods below.


“You don’t have anything to worry about,” Maggie said to the dean, her voice tight. “I promise.”


He nodded once and then left.



—


Whatever lightness she had seen in Arthur over the weekend was gone when he arrived at their office. It was replaced with a tense scrunch she recognized well. He set a paper cup from Bean There, Done That on her desk, along with a crinkling paper bag filled with a cream-cheese pastry. “Morning,” he said quietly, the air between them already thick with tension as he bent down and kissed her gently on the forehead.


Her anger was a weak thing, but her shame still burned. It wasn’t only shame at Dean Clearwater’s suspicion, at everything he left unsaid during his visit to her office that morning, but also shame at what she had done to Arthur. She had always known this relationship between them wouldn’t work, had always known it was a mistake, but she had done it anyway.


She stared at her computer. She was supposed to be reading through her notes on the incantation, but the words were swimming in front of her as tears pricked at the corners of her eyes. She didn’t know how to start this conversation. She didn’t know how to go on without having it. He had agreed—to keeping their relationship between them, to not go to Dean Clearwater about the budget—and why couldn’t he have just done what she asked? Why did he think he knew better?


Maggie was drawn back in her memory to Dr. Fleet’s office, when she went there to plead her case. But Evan had gotten there first. Evan has already let me know that you were struggling. That he has been helping you stay afloat for a year now. Between them, it had been Evan who’d struggled. She had coaxed him through long nights of panic about the quality of his work, motivating him to finish, prompting him to help him come up with ideas. Everything she had done to help him, he had turned on its head and used it to make his case seem more believable. You should have come to me or another member of the faculty. We could have helped you then, but it’s too late now.


“You’re thinking very hard over there,” Arthur said, and she looked up to find him watching her. His work bag remained unpacked beside him, his coffee forgotten on his desk. She didn’t respond right away, because she didn’t even know where to start. She couldn’t tell where her anger at Arthur ended and her rage at Evan began. “Talk to me,” he urged. “Please. Something happened on Saturday night. Just talk to me about it.”


She pushed the file folder across the desk. “Dean Clearwater dropped this off this morning.” He opened it but closed it quickly when he realized what was inside. “Your grant is fully approved.” She hated the flatness in her voice. She hated everything about this.


“I was going to tell you.”


Gods below, she had been a fool to think, even for a moment, that this could work. She should have learned her lesson with Evan, but here she was again, repeating her mistakes. “I told you not to talk to the dean. I told you we would figure it out together after we dissipated the pall.”


“I fixed it,” he pleaded. “I just wanted to make it right.”


She shook her head. “I told you how to make it right!”


“Maggie—”


“Did you stop to think, even for one second, how it would look to the dean if you took twelve thousand dollars of your own money to pay for one of my programs?”


He tensed. “What did he say to you?”


“It doesn’t matter! Did you think about it before you went to him?”


His eyes widened, and he started to say something but then stopped himself. “No,” he admitted, but no apology followed.


Her ears burned hot as she added, “Did you tell your family about me?” Her emotions were curled together—sadness, anger, shame—and too hard to extricate from one another. It would have been so much easier if she were just angry. “About us?”


His head fell back as if he were exhausted, and he closed his eyes. “They’re my family.” He sounded frustrated, resigned to whatever she had decided.


“I asked you not to do that, too,” she said in a calm, quiet voice she didn’t recognize. “They didn’t need to know we were sleeping together. I don’t tell my family every time I end up fucking a friend.”


It was a horrid thing to say. She wanted to take it back. She wanted to go back in time and reach into the air to grab the words before Arthur heard them. He made a small sound, like a gasp or a laugh, she couldn’t tell what. He turned around to look at her with a sharp, hurt expression.


His voice was cold when he said, “You told Dahlia the second I was out of your sight.”


“That’s not the same thing.”


“Isn’t it?”


“I told you that you could tell Rory. Rory, that’s it. So why did Lane come up and beg me not to break your heart?” Arthur groaned in frustration, and she looked away so she could get out the rest of what she needed to say. “You don’t take coworkers you’re casually sleeping with to the family celebration dinner. You don’t introduce them to your lovely stepmom and dad or your sweet nephew.”


When she finally looked back at him, she almost broke at the pain on his face. She had never wanted to hurt him, not even in her anger, but he had to understand that it would be so much worse the longer this went on. It was clear they couldn’t manage dating and working together, but maybe they could still salvage a working relationship as friends. And if not friends, then colleagues. After all, it had only been a few weeks over the summer, a fling…They could still manage being coworkers. Couldn’t they?


Despite it all, she couldn’t turn off her desire to comfort him, to find relief in his touch. She wanted to reach over her desk and kiss away his furrowed brow, ease the tension along his jawline with her fingers. But she didn’t. She stayed in her chair. She burrowed deeper in her anger.


“What are you afraid of?” he demanded, a hard edge to his pleading.


“I told you how we could make this work, over and over again. You just didn’t listen.”


She was surprised when his expression contorted in anger again. “Oh, c’mon. That’s bullshit. You never gave this, never gave us, a chance. There has been an expiration date on this from the moment you kissed me in that tent.”


“Exactly!” she nearly yelled. “I told you what this was, from the very first day. I told you what it could be, what I could give you. And you didn’t hear me. You heard what you wanted to.”


Arthur ran his fingers through his hair, like he just needed something to do with his hands. “I’m not him,” he said.


She stiffened and said, more to herself than Arthur, “I never should have let it get this far.” She knew he wasn’t Evan, but if he couldn’t see how he had broken her trust, hadn’t even bothered to say sorry…She had wanted to believe that Evan was uniquely awful, but maybe he wasn’t. Her breath caught, a sob stuck in her throat, as she had the horrible thought that maybe Evan wasn’t the problem at all. Maybe it was her. “That was my fault. And we should have had more time, but I think—”


“What are you saying?” he asked, a desperate edge to his voice.


“When the gloaming creeper decoction is done settling and we say our incantation, the pall will be gone. You’ll be able to move back into your office next week.”


He closed his eyes, as if he couldn’t stand to look at her.


“This has to end. Now,” she went on. “Before we hurt each other more. Before our lives are too intertwined.” Above and below, she already missed him. Her arms ached for him, despite her anger. And she just wanted to say his name, one last time. “I don’t want a break to destroy us, Arthur.”


After today, he should be Dr. Taliesin again. It would be fine. It would hurt the first few times, but it would be fine in the end. She had almost convinced herself.


“You’re already…” he began, his voice cracking, but he swallowed the words. When he spoke again, his voice was whisper quiet. “It will be enough for you?”


Maggie tried to find it in her heart to answer yes, but said instead, “It has to be.” She tried to look resolved. She tried to look sure. But Arthur’s furrow softened, just for a moment, at whatever he saw in her face instead.


He continued to stare at her for a moment, his gaze penetrating and hurt. She wasn’t sure what she wanted him to do. Apologize, to start, but then what? Fight for her? Yell at her? Tell her she was giving up too soon?


Instead, he gave her exactly what she said she wanted. “I’ll be out of here by the end of the week.” He gathered his bag, his now-cold coffee. When he stood and stepped around her desk, he paused when they were just inches apart. She looked up at him, eyes wide, as he said quietly, “Can I kiss you goodbye at least? One last time?”


She should have said no, but before she could get the word out, she was nodding. He leaned down, his hand steadying her rolling chair, and pressed his lips to hers, soft and tender. Tears were falling down her cheeks, but she wasn’t even sure when she’d started crying. She could taste them as she opened her lips for Arthur, just for a moment.


A sob built in her throat as Arthur’s hand came up to her face, gently stroking the tears from her cheeks, and she couldn’t bear the tenderness of his touch. When she pulled away, she slid her seat back just enough so he would have to step forward to touch her again. “Goodbye, Arthur,” she said, with a finality she didn’t feel. That she didn’t want.


His face collapsed, but he turned and left the office, closing the door behind him.

facts.fact: 周一独处：Lane 的话循环播放——要么他告诉了 Lane，要么她的爱意明显到被猜到。
facts.anchor: Either Arthur had told Lane about her

facts.fact: 她的噩梦推演：若不能并肩工作他会离开 Hawthorn——她不能把他从家人身边夺走。
院长突袭：grant 已过董事会全款到位——apparently 有预算错误，你知道吗。
暗示定罪：你是找 Taliesin 抱怨错误吗——受害者被一键改写成教唆者。
facts.anchor: did you complain to Dr. Taliesin about the error?

facts.fact: grant 详情：年度 twelve thousand dollars 捐给她 seminar、比原拨款还多；钱从哪来——他自己掏的。
关键证词：你不是我的首选——办公室分配是 Taliesin 定的，劝他 reconsider 他坚持。
Fleet 办公室闪回：Evan 先到一步说他帮你撑了一年——真相是挣扎的是 Evan；她陪他熬过一切被倒打一耙。
facts.anchor: helping you stay afloat for a year now

facts.fact: 最狠一句：我不是每次跟朋友上床都汇报家人；他冷回你我一转身就告诉了 Dahlia——Isn't it?。
保质期指控：从你在帐篷里吻我那刻起就有保质期——你没听见你想听的。
至暗推论：也许 Evan 不是问题——也许我是。
分手宣言：在生命缠得太深之前结束——Above and below 她已经开始想念他。
facts.anchor: Before our lives are too intertwined

facts.fact: 告别之吻：至少让我吻你道别最后一次——泪落进吻里；她后滑椅子 Goodbye, Arthur——finality 是装的；他关门离开。
facts.anchor: Can I kiss you goodbye at least? One last time?
